title: Can Computers Think? — Map 1 small-region reconstruction
subtitle: Boxes 59–65: heads-in-the-sand, theology, and arithmetic

regions.label: Should we pretend computers will never be able to think?
Does God prohibit computers from thinking?

nodes.label: The heads-in-the-sand objection.
nodes.text: Machine thought is rejected because its possible consequences are feared rather than because of an argument about what machines can do.
nodes.author: Alan Turing

nodes.label: The transmigration consolation.
nodes.text: Turing treats the fear behind the objection as calling for consolation rather than refutation and invokes the possibility of souls passing to machines.
nodes.author: Alan Turing

nodes.label: The theological objection.
nodes.text: The objection holds that thinking requires an immortal soul and that machines have not been given souls.
nodes.author: Alan Turing

nodes.label: The theological objection is ungrounded.
nodes.text: Turing rejects as arbitrary the assumption that machines could not receive souls and suggests that building thinking machines need not conflict with divine purposes.
nodes.author: Alan Turing

nodes.label: Computers can't add, much less think.
nodes.text: The claim distinguishes formal symbol manipulation from understood arithmetic: computational operations become mathematics only through interpretation.
nodes.author: Stanley L. Jaki; Fred Dretske
nodes.notes: Horn attributes the box to Jaki (1969) and Dretske (1990), and notes an earlier Wittgenstein version.

nodes.label: Computers can learn to add.
nodes.text: A computer with internal semantic structure may acquire arithmetic understanding through learning rather than possessing that understanding intrinsically.
nodes.author: William Rapaport

nodes.label: The marijuana-sniffing dog.
nodes.text: Meaningful thought requires symbols or signals to have the right causal role; a trained response by itself does not establish understanding.
nodes.author: Fred Dretske
